## Abstract

Transcriptional coregulators and transcription factors (TFs) contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that are critical for their association and function in gene regulation. More recently, IDRs have been shown to promote multivalent protein-protein interactions between coregulators and TFs to drive their association into condensates. In contrast, here we demonstrate how the IDR of the corepressor LSD1 excludes TF association, acting as a dynamic conformational switch that tunes repression of active cis-regulatory elements. Hydrogen-deuterium exchange shows that the LSD1 IDR interconverts between transient open and closed conformational states, the latter of which inhibits partitioning of the protein’s structured domains with TF condensates. This autoinhibitory switch controls leukemic differentiation by modulating repression of active cis-regulatory elements bound by LSD1 and master hematopoietic TFs. Together, these studies unveil alternative mechanisms by which disordered regions and their dynamic crosstalk with structured regions can shape coregulator-TF interactions to control cis-regulatory landscapes and cell fate.

## Abstract

Waterbury et al. show that the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of LSD1 autoinhibits its adjacent structured domains, blocking them from driving partitioning with diverse transcription factors (TFs). The IDR functions as a fuzzy molecular switch to regulate TF interactions, cis-regulatory landscapes, and cell fate.

## Introduction

Transcriptional coregulators are recruited by transcription factors (TFs) through a broad spectrum of mechanisms to control gene expression. Coregulators can directly bind TFs via high-affinity shape-complementary interactions mediated by specific protein domains and motifs, conferring cognate molecular recognition that can drive precise TF programs. A well-known example includes the LXXLL motif, which is recognized by nuclear receptors to recruit coregulators to affect ligand-gated transcriptional programs.1,2 Amenable to structural resolution, these high-affinity “lock and key” interactions have been extensively characterized.1,3–7 Moreover, the high level of TF-coregulator specificity afforded by these localized and structurally constrained “hotspot” interactions have provided tractable opportunities for their pharmacological disruption,8–11 and hence understanding the logic of TF-coregulator interactions will accelerate therapeutics development.

On the other end of the spectrum, coregulators can be broadly recruited through weak multivalent interactions. As opposed to structured motifs, these multivalent interactions are often mediated by the transactivation and repression domains of TFs, which are typically charged and intrinsically disordered.12–15 16–19 Moreover, IDRs of TFs, coregulators, and components of the general transcriptional machinery can drive their local concentration into macromolecular assemblies on chromatin.12–15,20–27 From here on, we will refer to these assemblies as either condensates or hubs. The molecular grammar of IDRs guiding the formation of condensates and the selective partitioning of factors within them have been extensively investigated,22,25,28,29 revealing properties such as amino acid composition or patterned blocks of residues that influence these processes. Condensates can also impart specificity by excluding factors.22,23 But in contrast to structured interactions, there remains a lack of mechanistic understanding on how IDRs achieve TF-coregulator selectivity. Structured domains can also drive condensate formation,25,30–34 and hence understanding their molecular interplay with IDRs in the context of full-length proteins is critical. Additionally, IDRs can also participate in autoregulatory contacts to directly mediate protein function, including enzyme activity, nucleic acid binding, oligomerization, and phase separation.35–37 For instance, the N-terminal IDR of p53, when phosphorylated, can contact and autoinhibit its neighboring DNA binding domain to control chromatin association. Uncovering the diverse mechanisms by which IDRs regulate TF-coregulator function will be essential towards understanding their impact on gene regulation.38

Contrasting modes of TF-coregulator recruitment are exemplified by the histone lysine demethylase LSD1, a corepressor that not only silences specific TF sites but also acts as a master regulator of cis-regulatory elements. LSD1 can be recruited to enhancers by the SNAG (SNAIL-GFI1) family TFs, including GFI1B, which bind the LSD1 active site with high affinity via their N-terminal SNAG domain.39,40 This high-affinity association is critical for hematopoiesis.41 Recruitment of LSD1 by GFI1B silences its cognate sites and is essential for normal erythroid and megakaryocytic differentiation, antagonizing myeloid TFs C/EBPα and PU.1, which commit cells to predominantly granulocytic or monocytic lineages.41–43 This TF antagonism operates in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and underlies the mechanism of action of many LSD1 inhibitors. Although LSD1 inhibitors were originally developed to block LSD1 enzyme activity, their antiproliferative effects in AML result from disrupting the protein-protein interaction between LSD1 and GFI1B. Dissociation of LSD1-GFI1B from chromatin results in activation of myeloid programs regulated by C/EBPα and PU.1 that drive differentiation (Figure 1A).8,43–45 Thus, beyond its canonical demethylase activity, LSD1 has nonenzymatic, TF-specific scaffolding functions where it recruits CoREST (i.e., RCOR1) and HDAC1/2 to suppress transcriptional activities essential for hematopoiesis.

Aside from repressing specific TF-target sites (e.g., GFI1B), LSD1 broadly localizes to active cis-regulatory elements, including super enhancers—genomic regions reflective of active transcriptional condensates. At these regions, LSD1 may be poised to decommission (i.e., silence) enhancers during processes like differentiation, or function more broadly as a global rheostat for enhancer and transcriptional activity.46–49 However, the factors that control LSD1 enhancer association and silencing remain unclear. More broadly, LSD1 and CoREST fall into a class of corepressors that counterintuitively localize to active cis-regulatory elements to repress gene activity.50 Owing to the high effective concentration of TFs at cis-regulatory elements, one possibility is that active transcriptional condensates may partition these corepressors through multivalent interactions, despite their opposing effects on transcriptional activity, in order to tune gene activity.20,21,27,51 To explore these possibilities, we investigated the molecular mechanisms governing LSD1-TF association and enhancer silencing.

Here we unveil an unanticipated mechanism by which the LSD1 N-terminal IDR tunes repression of active cis-regulatory elements and AML differentiation. Using a chemical genetics approach, we identify deletion mutations in the LSD1 IDR that confer resistance to LSD1 inhibitors as well as GFI1B depletion. We further find that disruption of the LSD1-GFI1B interaction redistributes LSD1 to lower-affinity TF partners, including C/EBPα. Leveraging these findings together, we discover that the LSD1 IDR negatively regulates the association of LSD1 with the IDRs of C/EBPα and additional master TFs by blocking its adjacent structured domains. Using hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that the LSD1 IDR is dynamic and masks these structured domains through transient interactions to control their accessibility and restrain promiscuous TF association. The LSD1 IDR may act to screen low-affinity TFs and specify repression of active cis-regulatory elements, including those involved in AML differentiation. This study demonstrates that autoinhibitory interactions between structured domains and IDRs can shape TF-coregulator interactions, cis-regulatory landscapes, cell fate, and drug action.

## Results

### LSD1’s IDR controls AML differentiation

We previously employed CRISPR-suppressor scanning to identify single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting LSD1 that confer drug resistance to the covalent LSD1 inhibitor named GSK-LSD1 (Figures 1A, 1B, S1A, and S1B).8 As anticipated, many sgRNAs targeting the LSD1 active site resulted in mutations that abrogate inhibitor binding (Figures 1B and S1B, blue dots). However, several inhibitor-enriched sgRNAs unexpectedly targeted regions distal to the LSD1 active site, including the LSD1 N-terminal IDR (amino acids (aa) 1–170) as well as a C-terminal surface-exposed loop (aa 770–795) (Figures 1B and S1B, red dots). To explore these findings, we transduced the AML cell line SET-2 with individual sgRNAs targeting these regions, treated with GSK-LSD1, and expanded drug-resistant clones harboring in-frame deletions, including (1) LSD1 G46_P52del, (2) LSD1 P77_G86del, and (3) LSD1 G788_P790del, hereafter referred to as NΔ1, NΔ2, and ΔGAP, respectively (Figures 1C and S1C–S1G). In comparison to wild-type (WT), when treated with GSK-LSD1, these mutant cell lines were drug resistant and exhibited reduced expression of CD86—a myeloid differentiation marker upregulated upon LSD1 inhibition (Figures 1D and 1E).44 Consistent with these findings, shRNA-mediated knockdown of endogenous LSD1 followed by overexpression of LSD1 NΔ1 or NΔ2 rescued growth in the presence of the inhibitor (Figure 1F). Taken together, these data implicate regions outside of the LSD1 active site, most notably the IDR, in AML differentiation and drug mechanism of action.

We next asked which step of the antiproliferative mechanism the IDR influences. Purified LSD1 IDR mutants were active in demethylation assays and their enzymatic activity was inhibited by GSK-LSD1, demonstrating that the mutations do not abrogate demethylase activity or inhibitor binding despite conferring drug resistance phenotypically in SET-2 cells (Figures S1H and S1I). Consistent with this, inhibitor treatment induced LSD1-GFI1B dissociation in both wild-type and IDR-mutant cells (Figure 1G). These results suggest that the IDR-mutant cells no longer require GFI1B altogether. In support, GFI1B depletion inhibited growth of wild-type but not IDR-mutant cells while LSD1 depletion caused comparable growth defects in both cell lines (Figure 1H). Collectively, these results indicate that LSD1 has additional functions in terminal differentiation, beyond its enzymatic activity and association with GFI1B, that are dependent on its IDR.

### Deletion mutations alter LSD1 condensation and TF partners

The LSD1 IDR comprises 20% of the LSD1 protein coding sequence but has few known functions.52,53 The IDR is primarily hydrophobic and the NΔ1 and NΔ2 mutations remove hydrophobic stretches enriched in glycine and proline (Figure 2A). We tested whether purified LSD1 and/or its IDR form droplets in vitro.25 Full-length LSD1-mCherry formed spherical droplets, which freely diffused, underwent fusion events, and scaled in size with protein concentration and inversely in size with increasing buffer ionic strength (Figures 2B, 2C, and S2A–S2F).14,15,20–27 These results indicate that LSD1 can form condensates in vitro.

Strikingly, the NΔ1 and NΔ2 deletions enhanced droplet formation (Figures 2B and 2C). By contrast, removal of the IDR (LSD1 ΔIDR) led to formation of insoluble aggregates. Pre-complexation of LSD1 ΔIDR with CoREST yielded well-formed droplets, suggesting that the IDR is not necessary for droplet formation and that the structural regions of the LSD1-CoREST complex can mediate condensate formation in vitro (Figure 2D). IDR alone only formed droplets at higher protein concentrations (Figure 2E), further suggesting that the structured domains contribute to phase separation of full-length LSD1. Consistent with this idea, the structured domains, particularly the active site, are highly negatively charged (Figure S2G).54 Lastly, we investigated LSD1 distribution in cells by creating U2OS knock-in cell lines that express endogenous LSD1 fused to monomeric enhanced GFP (LSD1-GFP). Wild-type and NΔ2-mutant LSD1-GFP displayed a mainly diffuse nucleoplasmic localization with a few small puncta per cell (Figure S2H). Together, the IDR influences LSD1’s propensity to engage in multivalent interactions and the structured domains might facilitate this phenomenon.

Since deletions in the IDR alter AML differentiation and LSD1 multivalency, we asked if these phenomena may be linked by altering LSD1 protein-protein interactions in cells. To identify LSD1 interactors that change upon GSK-LSD1 treatment, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of LSD1 in wild-type and NΔ2-mutant cells and measured interacting proteins by mass spectrometry (MS). As expected, inhibitor treatment did not significantly perturb the core LSD1-CoREST complex (i.e., RCOR1, HDAC1/2, PHF21A, HMG20A/B, GSE1) and the LSD1-GFI1B interaction was disrupted in both wild-type and mutant cells (Figures S2I and S2J). Unexpectedly, inhibitor treatment promoted LSD1’s interaction with several TFs, including C/EBPα, PU.1, and RUNX1 (Figures 2F and S2I). In fact, C/EBPα was the most up-regulated interactor in both cell lines, with modest enrichment in NΔ2 over wild-type. We validated LSD1’s interactions with key TFs identified by co-IP/MS in wild-type, NΔ1-, and NΔ2-mutant cells by co-IP of LSD1 followed by immunoblot. Both NΔ1 and NΔ2 LSD1 demonstrated stronger interactions with TFs, including C/EBPα, RUNX1, and GFI1B, than the wild-type counterpart (Figure S2J). Notably, C/EBPα and PU.1 act as key downstream effectors for LSD1 inhibitor-induced differentiation,8,43–45 and in agreement with prior studies in other AML models, knockdown of C/EBPα and PU.1 blocked CD86 upregulation by GSK-LSD1 in SET-2 cells (Figure 2G). Thus, inhibitor treatment reprograms LSD1-TF interactions, disrupting LSD1-GFI1B to induce LSD1-C/EBPα association (Figure 2H), and deletions in the IDR alter the relative recruitment of LSD1 to other TF partners.

While the association of LSD1 with the GFI1B SNAG domain has been previously described,8,40 the LSD1-C/EBPα interaction has yet to be characterized (Figure 2H). The N-terminus of C/EBPα comprises intrinsically disordered transactivation domains, which interact with various coregulators (Figure 2l).55,56 Hence, we hypothesized that C/EBPα could associate with LSD1 through weak multivalent interactions. Consistent with this idea, the IDR of C/EBPα fused to GFP partitioned into LSD1-mCherry droplets while GFP alone did not (Figures 2J, 2K and S2K). Droplets formed by NΔ1 and NΔ2 mutants displayed enhanced co-partitioning. Although LSD1 and C/EBPα co-partition into droplets, whether their association reflect discrete protein-protein interactions is unclear. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that LSD1 associates with C/EBPα and this is enhanced by the IDR mutations.

### LSD1’s IDR blocks association of lower-affinity TF partners

We next compared LSD1-TF interactions in cells and the role of the LSD1 IDR. We employed a LacO-LacI recruitment system in U2OS cells containing an integrated LacO array and either endogenous full-length LSD1-GFP or NΔ2-mutant LSD1-GFP knock-in, where the intensity of GFP signal at the LacO locus correlates with LSD1 association with the IDR-LacI tether (Figure 3A).12 We compared recruitment of wild-type versus NΔ2-mutant LSD1-GFP to the LacO array by LacI-mCherry constructs fused to the IDRs of either (1) GFI1B, which includes the high-affinity LSD1-binding SNAG sequence8,40 or (2) C/EBPα, which we refer to as GFI1B IDR-LacI and C/EBPα IDR-LacI, respectively. Both GFI1B IDR-LacI and C/EBPα IDR-LacI formed large LacO-associated foci where higher concentrations of the TF IDR-LacI were localized compared to LacI-mCherry foci (Figures S3A and S3B).12 In accordance with prior terminology,12,57–59 we refer to large LacO-associated foci as TF hubs, which serve as model systems for condensates. GFI1B IDR-LacI hubs strongly recruited LSD1, which was blocked by inhibitor treatment, consistent with the high-affinity LSD1-GFI1B interaction (Figures 3B, 3C, and S3B). By contrast, C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs recruited less LSD1, and this interaction was not impacted by inhibitor treatment (Figures 3D and 3E). These data indicate a distinct and weaker LSD1-C/EBPα interaction compared to LSD1-GFI1B. In agreement, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments revealed significantly greater residence time and total bound fraction for LSD1 at GFI1B IDR- versus C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs (Figures 3F and S3C), consistent with a significantly weaker and dynamic LSD1-C/EBPα interaction compared to LSD1-GFI1B.

While enrichment of wild-type and NΔ2-mutant LSD1 at GFI1B IDR-LacI hubs was comparable, NΔ2 was significantly more enriched at C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs versus wild-type (Figures 3B–3E). Moreover, LSD1 NΔ2 also had an increased total bound fraction at the C/EBPα IDR-LacI hub (Figure S3C). The residence time of LSD1 at either TF-LacI hub, or elsewhere in the nucleoplasm in the absence of recruitment, was not appreciably altered (Figures 3F and S3C–S3E). Altogether, these results demonstrate distinct mechanisms for LSD1 recruitment—high-affinity recruitment by GFI1B versus low-affinity recruitment by C/EBPα—and establish a key role of the LSD1 IDR in controlling the C/EBPα-bound fraction.

We next investigated whether the LSD1 IDR is necessary for C/EBPα association. Strikingly, LSD1 ΔIDR enriched at even greater levels at C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs compared to full-length and IDR mutants, demonstrating that the LSD1 IDR inhibits rather than drives C/EBPα association (Figures 3G, S3F, S3G, and S3H). Droplet experiments with recombinant C/EBPα IDR-GFP and LSD1-mCherry/CoREST, where complexation with CoREST solubilizes LSD1 ΔIDR droplets, were consistent with these findings (Figures 3H, 3I, and S3I). Altogether, these data demonstrate that the LSD1 IDR autoinhibits C/EBPα association. Since C/EBPα is necessary for AML differentiation, we reasoned that the IDR deletions may disrupt this autoinhibition, increasing LSD1-C/EBPα association to confer drug resistance. shRNA-mediated knockdown of endogenous LSD1 followed by overexpression of ΔIDR mutants, LSD1(Δ150) and LSD1(Δ170), rescued growth in the presence of GSK-LSD1 in SET-2 cells (Figures 3J). We validated these effects in other AML cell lines, including MV4;11, MOLM-13, and THP-1 (Figure S3J). Taken together, the LSD1 IDR inhibits LSD1-C/EBPα association to control AML differentiation.

### A bifunctional protein architecture controls TF co-condensation

To determine which regions of LSD1 associate with C/EBPα, LSD1 truncations were tested for partitioning into C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs (Figure 4A). The truncation containing structured domains—the amine oxidase domain (AOD) and tower domain—was sufficient for recruitment. By contrast, the LSD1 IDR alone was excluded. Additionally, LSD1 ΔIDR partitioned more readily than wild-type LSD1 into LacO-associated hubs formed by full-length or DNA binding domain (DBD) C/EBPα-LacI, suggesting that the structured DBD of C/EBPα also contributes to LSD1 recruitment in cells (Figures S4A and S4B). Together, LSD1’s IDR and structured domains have opposing propensities to interact with C/EBPα-LacI-hubs.

To assess divergent partitioning of LSD1 domains more broadly, we measured association of full-length LSD1, LSD1 ΔIDR, and LSD1 IDR alone across a panel of IDR-LacI hubs (24 TF/chromatin factor IDRs) (Figures 4B and S4C–S4E), where TF IDRs were selected to represent previously identified IDR classes.26 Generally, full-length LSD1 partitioned less into the IDR-LacI hubs in comparison to LSD1 ΔIDR and exclusion of the LSD1 IDR was weakly anti-correlated to inclusion of LSD1 ΔIDR (Figures 4C and 4D), suggesting that biophysical properties that repel the IDR also attract the structured domain. These trends were particularly striking for several IDR-LacI hubs formed by master TFs, like C/EBPα, RUNX1, GATA1, PU.1, MYB, and SOX2 (Figures 4F, S4F, and S4G). Beyond our co-IP/MS, many of these TFs have been previously demonstrated to interact with LSD1.43,46,60–63 To investigate whether LSD1 colocalizes with these endogenous TFs in cells, we assessed published K562 ChIP data to quantify LSD1 signal at TF binding sites. LSD1 signal is strongly enriched over input, particularly at GATA1 peaks (Figure 4E). Notably, the LSD1 IDR-LacI hub displayed minimal partitioning with LSD1 (Figure 4B), suggesting that the IDR and structured domains do not strongly interact. Altogether, these data reveal a bifunctional protein architecture of LSD1, where the structured domains drive partitioning with diverse TF hubs while the IDR mediates exclusion.

We evaluated if other enhancer-associated corepressors might possess bifunctional architectures that control TF co-condensation.47 We tested domains from CHD4 and HDAC1, corepressors previously shown to localize to active enhancers.47,64 While the IDRs of several corepressors are partially depleted from C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs, the adjacent structured domain of CHD4 partitioned into them (Figures 4G and S4H). This suggests that bifunctional architectures containing opposing unstructured and structured domains may be more broadly employed to control partitioning into condensates localized at active cis-regulatory elements.

A bifunctional protein architecture could control TF partitioning through multiple mechanisms. In particular, the IDR and structured domains could operate in trans (i.e., as separate independent modules) or in cis (i.e., cooperative mechanism). Noting that the LSD1 IDR weakly associates with its structured domains (LSD1 ΔIDR) (Figure 4B), we considered two mechanisms by which the LSD1 IDR could inhibit TF association: by (1) exclusion independent of the structured domain (i.e., in trans) or (2) by shielding the structured domain through IDR-structured domain contacts when tethered (i.e., in cis) (Figure 4H).22 Consequently, to investigate the mechanism that the LSD1 IDR uses to control TF partitioning, we evaluated two mutants, where the LSD1 IDR sequence was randomly scrambled, for their ability to mediate (1) exclusion, as the IDR alone, and (2) inclusion, as part of full-length LSD1 with C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs.

We first measured the recruitment of the wild-type and scrambled mutants of the LSD1 IDR to C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs. Scrambling the IDR did not affect LSD1 IDR exclusion (Figures 4I, S4I, and S4J). Next, we measured the recruitment of full-length wild-type LSD1 in comparison to full-length constructs containing the randomly scrambled IDR sequences. Strikingly, full-length LSD1 containing scrambled IDR sequences displayed enhanced recruitment into C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs compared to wild-type (Figures 4I and S4K). In contrast to the IDR alone, this shows that amino acid positioning of the IDR in the context of full-length LSD1 is a key determinant for TF association. The discrepancy between exclusion of the scrambled IDR alone and recruitment of full-length LSD1 containing the scrambled IDR demonstrate that the exclusionary properties of the wild-type LSD1 IDR alone is not sufficient to inhibit LSD1-C/EBPα interactions. Instead, the IDR and structured domains work in cis to control LSD1-TF interactions. To further test this idea, we evaluated a splice variant of the IDR containing a C-terminal 20 amino acid insert, isoform 2a, which has been demonstrated to alter cardiomyogenesis (Figures S4I–S4K).65 While the wild-type and isoform 2a IDRs displayed similar levels of exclusion, full-length LSD1 isoform 2a partitioned better into C/EBPα-LacI hubs than wild-type (Figure 4I). Collectively, these results show that the sequence and orientation of the IDR with respect to the structured regions control LSD1 partitioning.

### Dynamic states of the IDR control TF association

Our results point to a potential mechanism where intramolecular IDR-structured domain interactions control LSD1-TF recruitment. Moreover, the IDR and structured domains do not significantly interact in trans (Figure 4B), suggesting that the LSD1 bifunctional architecture may enforce weak contacts in cis through tethering. To probe the LSD1 IDR’s interplay with structured regions, we conducted hydrogen-deuterium exchange-mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) with full-length LSD1, ΔIDR, and NΔ1- and NΔ2-mutant complexes containing CoREST. Complete coverage was achieved for all mutants, enabling comprehensive mapping of their dynamics (Figure S5A). As anticipated, the average fractional deuterium uptake of full-length LSD1 revealed a dynamic IDR and C-terminus, which were both fully deuterated by 10 seconds, and a structured core. Notably, the IDR displayed bimodal HDX distributions along its entire length, indicating either distinct conformations or EX1 kinetics66 that occur when dynamic structural changes are slower than the exchange rate (Figures 5A, S5B and S5C). To differentiate between these possibilities, we labeled full-length LSD1 at higher time-resolution (Figures S5D and S5E). Deconvolution of the relative populations over time revealed an interconversion from a ‘closed’, exchange-incompetent state, to an ‘open’, exchange-competent state, characteristic of EX1 kinetics. Conformational switching from the ‘closed’ to the ‘open’ state was detected for all IDR peptides and was rapid, precluding full quantification of their distribution and half-lives (< 3 seconds, Figures S5D and S5E). Compared to full-length LSD1, mutations in the IDR resulted in increasingly larger fractions of the NΔ1- and NΔ2-IDRs in the open versus the closed state, as well as in higher deuterium uptake (Figures 5A–5C, S5B–S5C, S5F, and S6A–B). Altogether, these data show that the LSD1 IDR exists in dynamic yet distinct states with open states favored by the resistance mutations.

Strikingly, several regions of the LSD1-CoREST structured domains showed increased deuterium uptake for NΔ1-, NΔ2-, and ΔIDR-containing complexes in comparison to wild-type (Figures 5D, S5F, and S6A). These structured regions were common across all mutants, with the NΔ2 mutation increasing HDX to nearly commensurate levels as ΔIDR—which displayed the greatest difference. These data suggest that the highly dynamic IDR promotes transient, intramolecular interactions with the structured LSD1-CoREST core,67 which are disrupted by the deletion mutations (Figure 5E). However, we cannot rule out that increased accessibility of the IDR mutants may be attributed to wild-type LSD1-CoREST complex residing in a more stable conformation. Overlaying sites of increased HDX in the IDR mutants onto a prior X-ray crystal structure40 of LSD1 revealed regions throughout the resolved LSD1 core that gain accessibility with the mutants and highlight potential contact sites with the IDR (Figure 5F). These data support a mechanistic model where the closed state involves an IDR-structured domain contact interface, which when disrupted by mutations in the IDR (NΔ1, NΔ2), shifts the IDR toward the open state to increase the accessibility of the structured core (Figure 5E). By increasing the dynamics and accessibility of the LSD1 core, the structured domains of the IDR-mutants can more readily interact with TFs, such as C/EBPα. This model is consistent with our observations that full-length LSD1 constructs containing randomly scrambled IDR sequences or isoform 2a, both of which likely relieve IDR-structured domain occlusion, also enhanced partitioning with C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs (Figure 4I).

Notably, one of the structured regions that gained accessibility in the IDR mutants includes the surface-exposed loop where the ΔGAP resistance mutation is located (Figures 5D, 5F, and S5F). HDX-MS with ΔGAP LSD1-CoREST revealed broadly increased HDX in the structured domains compared to wild-type (Figure S5G). Moreover, increased protection from HDX in the GAP loop and the IDR was observed in the ΔGAP mutant, suggesting a direct contact between these two regions that can tune the accessibility of the structured core. Like the IDR mutants, LSD1 ΔGAP displayed increased partitioning with C/EBPα IDR-LacI hubs in comparison to wild-type (Figures 5G and S4K), demonstrating that deletion mutations in the structured domain (i.e., ΔGAP) and the IDR can both increase TF interactions, supporting that there is functional crosstalk between these regions. Collectively, these findings show that dynamic states of the IDR control TF association by modulating accessibility of the LSD1-CoREST structured domains rather than directly promoting IDR-IDR exclusion.

### LSD1 IDR attenuates active enhancer repression

Having established a role of the LSD1 IDR in autoinhibiting LSD1-TF association, we considered its ramifications on cis-regulatory elements in AML cells. Aside from repressing specific TF-target sites (e.g., GFI1B) through its direct high-affinity recruitment to chromatin, LSD1 occupies active cis-regulatory elements, including super enhancers.46,47 We asked if weaker LSD1-TF interactions regulated by the LSD1 IDR modulate the activity of these enhancers, and accordingly, we performed ChIP-seq for LSD1, CoREST (i.e., RCOR1), GFI1B, C/EBPα, RUNX1, PU.1 and H3K27ac—a histone modification enriched at active enhancers. Consistent with other cell types, LSD1 and CoREST occupy regions marked by H3K27ac in SET-2 cells (Figures 6A and 6B). We hypothesized that LSD1 complexes actively attenuate the enhancers they occupy through their corepressor activity and therefore reasoned that depletion of LSD1 will increase enhancer activation. Therefore, we conducted quantitative ChIP-seq (ChIP-Rx)67 for H3K27ac after acute depletion of LSD1-CoREST by 6 h treatment with UM171—a small molecule that degrades the LSD1-CoREST complex (Figure 6C).68 Consistent with our hypothesis, after UM171 treatment, broad increases in H3K27ac were observed and these increases were correlated with the initial levels of LSD1 (Figures 6D and S7A).

Because of its increased association with C/EBPα and other TFs, we considered if IDR-mutant LSD1 may aberrantly block enhancer activation caused by GSK-LSD1 treatment (Figure 6E).8,43–45 We mapped LSD1 and H3K27ac localization using ChIP-seq in wild-type and NΔ2-mutant SET-2 cells after vehicle or inhibitor treatment. Upon inhibitor treatment, disruption of LSD1-GFI1B binding was accompanied by increased LSD1 levels at other TF and H3K27ac sites (Figures S7B–S7E), supporting the notion that loss of the high-affinity LSD1-GFI1B interaction induces LSD1 redistribution to lower-affinity TF partners (Figures 2F and 2H). Despite the repressive function of LSD1 at active enhancers (Figure 6D), a concomitant increase in H3K27ac levels was observed across LSD1 sites co-bound by C/EBPα, PU.1, or RUNX1 in wild-type cells (Figures 6F and S7E), highlighting that wild-type LSD1 association cannot fully overcome TF-driven enhancer activation. By contrast, in NΔ2-mutant cells, increases in H3K27ac levels were blocked at these sites upon GSK-LSD1 treatment, suggesting that full enhancer activation is impaired by LSD1 NΔ2 (Figure 6F). Consistent with the requirement of enhancer activation for differentiation, co-treatment of GSK-LSD1 with the BET inhibitor JQ1, which inhibits enhancer activity, led to a dose-dependent reduction of CD86-positivity in SET-2 cells, indicating a block in myeloid differentiation (Figure 6G). Treatment with JQ1 at the same doses (25 and 50 nM) only impacted growth minimally in wild-type SET-2 cells (Figure S7F). Lastly, depletion of LSD1 NΔ2 by either CRISPR knockout (Figure 1H) or UM171 treatment still led to differentiation of NΔ2-mutant cells (Figure 6H), suggesting an active role of mutant LSD1 in suppressing differentiation. Taken together, these results indicate that LSD1 buffers active enhancers to control drug-induced AML differentiation and the LSD1 IDR plays a critical role by tuning the interactions with TF partners to maintain active chromatin. Increased association with TF partners caused by the IDR mutations instead result in aberrant enhancer repression that impedes differentiation (Figure 7).

## Discussion

IDRs are implicated in the formation of nuclear condensates to control gene expression and genome organization,15,69–72 but the molecular mechanisms dictating function and selectivity remain elusive due to challenges in studying disordered protein domains. Here we unveil how the IDR of LSD1 can engage in transient intramolecular interactions to autoinhibit protein function and control cell fate. Juxtaposition of the opposing IDR and structured domains in LSD1 gives rise to a bifunctional protein architecture; we further show that these domains cooperate in cis where the IDR sequence and position are critical. We leverage HDX-MS with functional mutants to capture IDR dynamics in the context of full-length proteins, demonstrating that the IDR interconverts between a closed inhibitory state and an open state where the structured domains are also accessible (Figure 7). Mutations in the IDR cause the open state to be favored, potentiating weak interactions with TFs by unmasking the structured regions of LSD1-CoREST. Our work shows how dynamic protein states involving an IDR, although short-lived, can control weaker interactions to form an autoinhibitory switch.

Intriguingly, as separate modules, the IDR is excluded from TF condensates while the structured domains are included, highlighting their intrinsic opposition. In contrast to “lock and key” type molecular switches involving specific, stable interactions,1–7 the contacts driving the closed autoinhibited state of LSD1 are weak and likely only driven by tethering of these otherwise opposing domains. Therefore, the IDR autoinhibitory switch is tuned to regulate weaker interactions, including those involved with condensates. In this capacity, the LSD1 IDR may have evolved to screen lower-affinity TFs away from the structured domain and confers TF specificity—protecting certain cis-regulatory elements from aberrant repression. Critically, this specificity includes master regulator TFs important for hematopoiesis (i.e., C/EBPα, PU.1, RUNX1, GATA1, MYB) and pluripotency (i.e., SOX2, OCT4), and the IDR likely regulates LSD1’s established roles in these cell processes.46,48 In contrast to lower-affinity TFs, high-affinity TFs like GFI1B override the IDR’s inhibitory function.

IDRs in RNA and chromatin binding proteins can behave as regulatory switches, often regulated by post-translational modifications like phosphorylation.34,38,73–76 Notably, phosphorylation of the LSD1 IDR has been demonstrated to alter specific TF programs, although further work is needed to discern if these effects are mediated by altering IDR-structured domain contacts.53,77 Altogether, our study raises the prospect that intramolecular IDR-structured domain crosstalk is more generally employed to tune coregulator function.

By comparing low- and high-affinity TF complexes, our study contextualizes the mechanistic spectrum and molecular logic by which corepressors and TFs interactions control cis-regulatory elements and cell differentiation. Although high-affinity hotspot interactions directly recruit LSD1 to silence cognate TF sites (i.e., GFI1B), weaker multivalent interactions with LSD1’s structured domains can facilitate association with TFs to repress active cis-regulatory elements, acting as a rheostat for active transcriptional condensates (Figure 7).49,78 Notably, GFI1B and C/EBPα are important TFs for hematopoiesis79–81 and LSD1 inhibitors also promote HSC expansion,82,83 further highlighting the critical role of the lineage TF switch delineated here. Critically, LSD1 falls within a larger class of corepressors, including CHD4, that localize to active cis-regulatory elements to repress gene activity,47–50,64,78 and hence the classes of mechanisms defined here may prove more general.

Using small molecules as precision tools to disrupt the high-affinity LSD1-GFI1B complex, we discern the molecular logic of LSD1-TF interactions and reveal broader principles of IDR function. From a practical perspective, these findings also offer important considerations for drug discovery, as the intended disruption of TF complexes can inadvertently form new ones that retain critical roles in drug action. More broadly, we demonstrate that the deep characterization of drug resistance mutations is not only useful for identifying sites of small molecule binding and/or allostery but can provide powerful reagents to interrogate structure-function and dissect the molecular and temporal steps in downstream mechanism of action.84 In summary, using chemical genetic approaches, we define a novel mechanism of IDR-structured domain antagonism, which controls LSD1 silencing of active enhancers and cell fate.

### Limitations of the study

In this study, we describe the weak interaction of LSD1 with several TFs (e.g., C/EBPα), however, the precise biophysical nature of these protein-protein interactions remains unclear. Additionally, the LacI-IDR recruitment system used to measure these weak interactions and model condensates is artificial and may not reflect the behavior of endogenous TFs. Deeper characterization of endogenous LSD1-TF interactions and how different TFs coordinate this activity within cells is warranted. Through HDX-MS, we show that the LSD1 IDR adopts distinct conformations to control association of its structured domains with TFs. As these conformations are highly transient, we cannot fully characterize and deconvolute their dynamics and relative half-lives. Deeper investigation is also needed to determine what factors control the conformational switch of the LSD1 IDR, such as post-translational modifications.53,77 Lastly, our study uses limited AML cell lines to study the role of LSD1 IDR. Additional investigations will be needed to determine the role of LSD1 IDR in more AML models and normal hematopoietic cells as well as during physiological processes like differentiation.

### Method Details

#### Chemical reagents

Compounds were in dissolved in DMSO and stored at −80 °C. The vehicle condition represents 0.1% (v/v) DMSO treatment. GSK-LSD1 and JQ1 were used purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (≥98% by HPLC).

#### Lentivirus preparation and transduction

Lentivirus was produced by co-transfecting HEK293T cells with pCMV-VSV-G, psPAX2 and transfer vector plasmid (encoding gene of interest) using FuGENE HD (Promega) or Lipofectamine 3000 according to manufacturers’ protocols. Media was exchanged after 6–7 h and the viral supernatant was collected 48–72 h post-transfection and filtered (0.45 μm). Transduction was carried out by mixing the virus with cells with 8 μg/ml polybrene for SET-2 and 5 μg/ml for U2OS and then spinfected at 1,800 × g for 90 min at 37 °C. After 48 h post-transduction, media was changed and puromycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) selection was carried out for 3 d at 2 μg/mL for SET-2 and U2OS.

#### Generation of clonal drug-resistant LSD1 mutant cell lines

sgRNA sequences targeting LSD1 to generate sgNΔ1, sgNΔ2, and sgΔGAP were cloned into pLentiCRISPR-eGFP or pLentiCRISPRv2-puro. SET-2 were transduced with the resultant plasmids as indicated above and subsequently treated with 100 nM GSK-LSD1 to enrich for drug-resistant mutant cells. Surviving cells were FACS-sorted as single cells and then expanded. For library preparation, genomic PCR primers with Illumina adapter sequences were used to amplify specified regions of LSD1. Samples were sequenced on a MiSeq genome analyzer (Illumina) and analyzed using CRISPResso2 (v.2.0.40).

#### Gene knockout by CRISPR/Cas9 and competition-based growth assays

pLentiGuide-mCherry was constructed by replacing the puromycin resistant gene in pLentiGuide-Puro (Addgene plasmid #52953). sgRNA sequences targeting LSD1 or GFI1B were cloned into pLentiGuide-mCherry. Cas9-expressing SET-2 WT, NΔ1 and NΔ2 cell lines were transduced with the resultant pLentiGuide-mCherry plasmids as indicated above. mCherry-positive cell population was mixed with non-transduced mCherry-negative SET-2 WT cells at 1:1 ratio at d4 post-infection The percentage of mCherry-positive was measured every 3–5 days up to 20 days using ACEA Novocyte flow cytometer (Agilent). Normalized percentage of mCherry+ cells was calculated by subtracting final time-point with the initial time.

#### shRNA-mediated knockdown of LSD1 followed by overexpression and competition-based growth assays

Site-directed mutagenesis as performed using Q5 Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (New England Biolabs) to generate LSD1 NΔ1, NΔ2, Δ150 and Δ170 and were subcloned into pSMALP-mCherry with an N-terminal FLAG tag using Gibson cloning (New England Biolabs). SET-2 were transduced with the resultant plasmids and sorted for mCherry+ cells. shRNA sequence targeting LSD1 was cloned into pLKO.1-puro. The mCherry+ cells were subsequently transduced with pLKO.1 shLSD1 to knock down LSD1. The mCherry+ cell population was mixed with mCherry-negative SET-2 shLuciferase cells at 1:1 ratio post-puromycin selection. Normalized percentage of mCherry+ cells was calculated by subtracting final time-point with the initial time.

#### siRNA knockdown

siRNA were purchased from ThermoFisher (Silencer Select siRNAs). SET-2 cells were electroporated with 200 nM siRNAs at 1400V with 20 ms pulse width for 2 pulses using the NEON system (Invitrogen).

#### Flow cytometry and analysis

Cell surface expression of CD86 and CD11b was measured by flow cytometry. Live cells were collected, washed once with PBS and stained with appropriate antibodies in staining buffer (PBS supplemented with 2% FBS). After 30 minutes of incubation at 4°C in the dark, cells were washed once with PBS and analyzed by flow cytometry (ACEA Novocyte, Agilent). Data were analyzed with FlowJo™ v10 software.

#### Genotype determination

Genomic DNA was isolated using QIAamp Blood & Cell Culture DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen). For amplicon sequencing, genomic DNA was subjected to two rounds of PCR reactions. First round of PCR was conducted using 500 ng of genomic DNA with Q5 HotStart Polymerase (NEB) to amplify the target region. PCR products were ran on an agarose gel and gel-purified using Zymo Gel Extraction Kit (Zymo). 1 uL of the purified DNA was used as an input for the second round of PCR. PCR was conducted with PCR primers containing Illumina adaptor sequences, and resultant products were ran on an agarose gel, gel purified and pooled. Samples were sequenced on a MiSeq genome analyzer (Illumina) and analyzed using CRISPResso2.

#### Mammalian overexpression constructs

To generate LSD1-mEGFP U2OS 2–6-3 overexpression cell lines, mEGFP followed by a ‘GGGSGGGS’ linker was cloned into the C-terminus of LSD1 harboring an N-terminal Flag-SV40 NLS tag followed by ‘GGS’ in pcDNA3.1 for transient transfection and then moved into an IRES puro lentiviral vector for stable overexpression. U2OS 2–6-3 cells were transduced and selected with puromycin as described above followed by immunoblot validation.

#### CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing

Knock-in cell lines were generated according to published procedures. mEGFP followed by a ‘GGGSGGGS’ linker was knocked into the C-terminus of LSD1 in U2OS 2–6-3 cells. sgRNA targeting the C-terminus of LSD1 was cloned into a Cas9 plasmid, PX459, and co-transfected with a repair vector containing the mEGFP CDS and linker flanked by 750 bp of genomic homology sequence of KDM1A C-terminus on either side. Cells were FACS-sorted on a MoFlo Astrios EQ cell sorter for GFP+ into 96-well plates, expanded, and screened by genomic PCR followed by validation with Sanger sequencing and western blot.

To generate U2OS 2–6-3 LSD1-mEGFP NΔ2, electroporation was performed using the NEON system with gRNA complex and Alt-R Cas9 enzyme from IDT. gRNA complex was formed by reconstituting gene-specific crRNA sgNΔ2 and tracrRNA (1072534, IDT) to 100 μM in IDT duplex buffer, mixed 1:1 and hybridized by incubation at 95°C for 5 min, followed by cooling to room temperature on the bench top. RNP complex was formed by mixing gRNA complex with Alt-R Cas9 enzyme and followed by incubation at room temperature for 15 min. 2 × 105 cells were washed twice with PBS and resuspended in buffer R. RNP complex, gene-specific Ultramer ssODN donor consisting of 50 bp on either side of the mutation and Alt-R Cas9 electroporation enhancer were added to the cell suspension and electroporated at 1400V with 15 ms pulse width for 4 pulses using the Neon Transfection System 10 μL kit (Thermo Fisher, MPK1025). After electroporation, cells were immediately transferred to prewarmed media supplemented with HDR Enhancer. To generate single-cell clones, cells were sorted on a MoFlo Astrios EQ cell sorter, expanded, and screened by genomic PCR followed by validation with Sanger sequencing.

#### Immunoblotting

For whole cell extracts, cells were lysed on ice using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (Boston BioProducts) supplemented with fresh HALT™ protease inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The lysate was clarified by centrifugation at 10,000 × g for 10 min. Protein concentration of the lysates was measured using Bradford Assay (Bio-rad) or BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Immunoblotting was performed according to standard procedures.

#### Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP)

2 × 107 SET-2 cells were washed with cold PBS and lysed on ice in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1% IGPAL-CA-630) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche) and the lysates were cleared. The protein concentration was quantified as above and diluted to 1 mg/mL in lysis buffer. Antibodies were crosslinked to Protein G Dynabeads (ThermoFisher Scientific) using BS3. Crosslinked Dynabeads were washed thrice with lysis buffer and incubated with the precleared protein lysate. Immunoprecipitation was carried out overnight at 4 °C under constant rotation. Beads were washed once with wash buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% IGPAL-CA-630) and twice with wash buffer B (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) and eluted in SDS-PAGE loading buffer and carried forward to immunoblotting as described above or mass spectrometry as described below.

#### Mass spectrometry

Beads were washed with 50 mM Tris HCl (500 μL, pH 7.5, 4X) and transferred to fresh 1.7 mL Eppendorf tubes (Axygen, MCT175LC) after the second and fourth washes. Proteins were digested off beads by adding 1 mM DTT (150 μL), 5 ug/mL Trypsin (Promega), 2 M urea, 50 mM Tris HCl digestion buffer and incubating for 1 hour at 25 °C, with shaking. The supernatant was removed and saved and an additional 150 μL of digestion buffer was added and incubated for 30 minutes at 25 °C, with shaking. The supernatants were combined, and the beads were washed with 2M Urea, 50 mM Tris HCl (150 μL, 2X), added to the saved supernatants, and transferred to fresh tubes for in-solution digestion. Proteins were reduced with 4 mM DTT, alkylated with 10 mM IAA, and digested with 0.5 ug of Trypsin overnight at 25°C, with shaking. The samples were quenched the following day with formic acid to a final concentration of 1% FA (pH < 3). Samples were desalted with C18 stage tips (2 punches) following standard protocol. Samples were loaded onto the tips and washed with 0.1% FA (100 μL, 2X) before eluting with 50% ACN, 0.1% FA (50 μL), frozen and lyophilized. Desalted samples were resuspended in 11 uL of 100 mM HEPES, pH 8.5, and labeled with 5 μL of TMT-11 reagent (Thermo Scientific, LOT# TE270748 - TD264064) at a concentration of 20 μg/μL in 100% ACN. The labeling reaction occurred at room temperature for 1 hour, with shaking. Conditions were as follows: LSD1 wild type, DMSO (126, 127N) and GSK-LSD1 (127C, 128N); NΔ2, DMSO (128C, 129N) and GSK-LSD1 (129C, 130N); WT/NΔ2, DMSO, rabbit IgG (130C, 131N). Samples were then diluted with 5 μL of 70 mM HEPES, 30% can, quenched with 5% Hydroxylamine (1 μL), combined, lyophilized, and resuspended with 3% ACN, 5% FA (150 μL). TMT-labeled samples were fractionated by high-pH C18 reverse phase fractionation (3 punches). 40 ug were loaded onto the stage tip and washed with 1% FA (100 μL, 2X). Following high-pH equilibration with 3% ACN, 20 mM ammonium formate (250 μL, 4X), six fractions were collected (300 μL each) in HPLC vials at 8%, 12%, 16%, 20%, 25% and 50%. Fractions were frozen, lyophilized and resuspended in 3% ACN/5% FA (8 μL) for MS analysis (2 μL).

Fractionated samples were analyzed on an Orbitrap Q-Exactive HF-X Plus MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a nanoflow ionization source and coupled to a nanoflow Proxeon EASY-nLC 1000 UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were injected on an in-house packed column (22cm × 75um diameter C18 silica picofrit capillary column) heated at 50 °C. The mobile phase flow rate was 250 nL/min of 3% ACN/1% FA (solvent A) and 90% ACN/ 0.1% FA (solvent B). Peptides were separated using the following LC gradient: 0–6% B in 1 min, 6–30% B in 85 min, 30–60% B in 9 min, 60–90% B in 1 min, stay at 90% B for 5 min, 90–50% B in 1 min, and stay at 50% B for 5 min. Data was acquired in centroid mode for both MS1 and MS2 scans. Samples were analyzed in data dependent analysis (DDA) mode using a Top-20 method. Ion source parameters were: spray voltage 2 kV, source temperature 250 °C. Full MS scans were acquired in the m/z range 350–1800, with an AGC target 3e6, maximum IT 10 ms and resolution 60,000 (at m/z 200). MS/MS parameters were as follows: AGC target 5e4, maximum IT 105 ms, loop count 20, isolation window 0.7 m/z, NCE 31, resolution 45,000 (at m/z 200) and fixed first mass 100 m/z; unassigned and singly charged ions were excluded from MS/MS.

Raw MS data were analyzed using Spectrum Mill Proteomics Workbench (prerelease version B.06.01.202, Agilent Technologies). A trypsin specific enzyme search was performed using a 2017 uniprot human fasta file (UniProt.human.20171228.RISnrNF.553smORFs.264contams) containing 65095 entries. Peptide and fragment tolerances were at 20 ppm, minimum matched peak intensity 40% and peptide false discovery rates (FDR) were calculated to be <1% using the target-decoy approach.99 Fixed modifications were carbamidomethylation, TMT 10 (N-term, K) and variable modifications were Acetyl (ProN-term), Oxidized methionine (M), Pyroglutamic acid (N-termQ) and Deamidation (N). Spectra with a score <4 were filtered out. Peptides were validated using the following parameters: for charge states 2–4, a FDR of 1.2 was applied to each run and for charge state 5, a FDR of 0.6 was applied across all runs. Results were further validated at the protein level and proteins with a score of 20 or higher were accepted as valid. Reporter ion correction factors, specific to the TMT batch, were applied. A protein/peptide summary was generated using the median across all TMT channels as the denominator. Shared peptides were assigned to the protein with the highest score (SGT). Calculated ratios at the protein level were imported into Protigy for normalization and features selection (https://github.com/broadinstitute/protigy). To account for variability between samples, log ratios were normalized by centering using the sample Median and scaled using the sample Median Absolute Deviation (Median MAD). A linear model was used to calculate the log fold change ((log2 (vehicle/Drug)) for NΔ2 and WT taking into account DMSO controls.

LSD1 enzymatic activity assays were performed in triplicate using Amplex Red Hydrogen Peroxide/Peroxidase Assay Kit (Invitrogen) with recombinant LSD1 and a synthetic peptide corresponding to the first 21 amino acids of H3K4me2 (Anaspec). Before acquiring all the fluorescence images, we set the laser intensity and microscope detectors to make sure no pixels in the images were saturated and for 2-color imaging, proper emission filters were used to ensure no channel bleed-through. Images presented are of droplets that have settled on the glass surface of the imaging plate. #### FRAP imaging

#### LacO-LacI confocal image quantification analysis

To quantify LSD1-GFP enrichment at the LacO arrays we followed previously reported protocols.27 Briefly, we selected a primary region of interest corresponding to the IDR-LacI-mCherry tether detected based on a fixed intensity threshold on the mCherry-channel using ZEN Blue 3.0. #### ChIP-seq Data Analysis

ChIP-seq data generated for this paper were analyzed by aligning paired-end reads to the GRCh38 human reference using the STAR (version 2.7.0e) aligner with splicing disabled. The resulting .bam file is duplicate-marked and down-sampled to comparable coverage using picard (version 2.22.3). Peaks for each replicate were called separately with HOMER (version 4.10) with matched inputs before establishing the final peak list with an irreproducible discovery rate (IDR) of 2%. Replicates were then merged and converted into bigwig files for visualization with deepTools2 (version 3.4.3) with the following parameters: --extendReads 200 --ignoreDuplicates --normalizeUsing BPM. ChIP peak profile plots and read-density heat maps were also generated using deepTools2 (version 3.4.3).

Bed files for GATA1, RUNX1, PU.1, LEF1, IKZF1, ETS, FUS, CBX5, H3K27ac and H3K27me3 binding peaks in K562 were downloaded from their respective GEO. Bed files that are originally aligned to GRCh37 were converted to GRCh38 using the UCSC liftOver webtool with default settings. Bed files with replicates were merged by obtaining overlapping peaks in both files using HOMER (version 4.10) mergePeaks. Reads for LSD1 ChIP-seq in K562 were downloaded from GEO and aligned to GRCh38 human reference using the STAR (version 2.7.0e) aligner with splicing disabled. The resulting .bam file is duplicate-marked using picard (version 2.22.3). Bigwig files of LSD1 (and corresponding input) were generated using deepTools2 (version 3.4.3) with the following parameters: --extendReads 200 --ignoreDuplicates --normalizeUsing BPM –binSize 25. For plotting of LSD1 signal at various TF binding sites, read density of LSD1 and input were calculated using deepTools2 (version 3.4.3). LSD1 and input signal in bins 500 bp centered upon middle of peak were then averaged, log2 + 1-transformed and subtracted from each other to obtain log2-fold change values. Box plots were generated using matplotlib (v.3.7.1).

#### Quantitative ChIP-seq Data Analysis

Paired-end reads were aligned to a composite reference genome for dm6 and hg38 utilizing bowtie2 (version 2.3.2) according to the Spiker analysis framework (version 1.03). The resulting .bam file is duplicate-marked and down-sampled to comparable coverage using picard (version 2.22.3). The Spiker split_bam.py script was run to calculate scaling factors and to split reads into an alignment file containing reads specifically aligning to the hg38 genome (Spiker, version 1.0.3)38. This alignment file was then converted into spike-in normalized bigwig file for further analysis and visualization utilizing the deepTools bamCoverage command with the following parameters: --binSize 50 –ignoreDuplicates--normalizeUsing RPKM --ignoreForNormalization chrM --extendReads –scaleFactor.

#### Analysis of LSD1 sequence features

Amino acid composition plots were generated using matplotlib (v.3.7.1). Net charge per residue of LSD1 amino acid sequence was calculated with the default settings of 5 amino acid sliding window using localCIDER (v.0.1.19). Predicted disorder values along the length of human LSD1 protein was determined using PONDR VLS2 algorithm. Higher values indicate greater predicted disorder.

Maps of basic and acidic patches were calculated based off previous studies.27 Briefly, amino acid compositions of basic and acidic residues were calculated in sliding 5-residue windows using localCIDER (v.0.1.19).; basic and acidic patches were defined as regions of ≥ 5 consecutive residues that consist of basic and acidic residues, respectively, occurring at a frequency of > 0.5. Plots were generated using matplotlib (v.3.7.1).

#### Data processing for CRISPR-suppressor scanning analysis

Published data were analyzed as previously described.8 Briefly, reads uniquely assigned to each sgRNA in the library were read-count normalized, log2 + 1 transformed, averaged across three replicates, and were then normalized by subtracting the average of the log2-transformed counts across three replicates of that sgRNA at week 0. Finally, for each condition the mean of the transformed counts for all functionally neutral genome-targeting control sgRNAs (averaged across replicates and normalized as described above) was subtracted from each the enrichment value of each sgRNA for that specific condition. Heatmaps showing sgRNAs with significant enrichment, with windows of 5 amino acids, were constructed using matplotlib (v.3.7.1).

#### Ranking of H3K27ac-marked regions and LOESS fit

H3K27ac peaks were called using HOMER (version 4.10) findPeaks with the following parameters: -style super -superSlope −1000 -tagThreshold 50. Read density for H3K27Ac, LSD1, and RCOR1 were calculated using HOMER annotatePeaks.pl with size parameter set to ‘given’. To generate input-normalized ChIP-seq signal, normalized input read counts were subtracted from the read counts of each factors, before the signal was normalized so that the maximum was 1.0 for each factor. The LOESS polynomial regression fit of input-normalized ChIP-seq signal was plotted against regions sorted and ranked by H3K27ac content using matplotlib (v.3.7.1).

# Integrative dissection of gene regulatory elements at base resolution

**Authors:** Zeyu Chen; Nauman Javed; Molly Moore; Jingyi Wu; Gary Sun; Michael Vinyard; Alejandro Collins; Luca Pinello; Fadi J. Najm; Bradley E. Bernstein

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA | 2Gene Regulation Observatory, Broad Institute, Cambridge, MA, USA | 3Department of Cell Biology and Pathology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 4Department of Pathology, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 5Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA

## Abstract

Although vast numbers of putative gene regulatory elements have been cataloged, the sequence motifs and individual bases that underlie their functions remain largely unknown. Here, we combine epigenetic perturbations, base editing, and deep learning to dissect regulatory sequences within the exemplar immune locus encoding CD69. We converge on a ∼170 base interval within a differentially accessible and acetylated enhancer critical for CD69 induction in stimulated Jurkat T cells. Individual C-to-T base edits within the interval markedly reduce element accessibility and acetylation, with corresponding reduction of CD69 expression. The most potent base edits may be explained by their effect on regulatory interactions between the transcriptional activators GATA3 and TAL1 and the repressor BHLHE40. Systematic analysis suggests that the interplay between GATA3 and BHLHE40 plays a general role in rapid T cell transcriptional responses. Our study provides a framework for parsing regulatory elements in their endogenous chromatin contexts and identifying operative artificial variants.

## Abstract

Chen and Javed et al. integrated epigenetic perturbations, base editing, and deep learning to dissect a CD69 enhancer. They identified a single C-to-T mutation that impacts gene expression by altering binding of GATA3, TAL1, and BHLHE40. Extending their analysis, they find evidence of a broader interaction between GATA3 and BHLHE40 during T cell activation.

## Introduction

Genome-wide maps of chromatin state and transcription factor (TF) binding have nominated more than a million cell type-specific regulatory elements (REs) in the human genome as potential context-specific regulators of gene expression.1,2,3 A critical next step is to determine their functions and sequence determinants. Computational tools that predict functional bases and/or gene targets are rapidly evolving but require systematic benchmarking against perturbational data.4,5 Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) enable high-throughput analysis of sequence determinants within REs but are based on exogenously introduced constructs that do not recapitulate the native chromatin contexts.6,7,8,9 CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) with fusions between dCas9 and the KRAB repressor provides a means to suppress an RE in its native context and evaluate consequent transcriptional changes.10,11,12,13,14 Traditional CRISPR-based genetic perturbations offer increased resolution15,16 but incur variable sequence changes due to heterogeneity of insertions or deletions (indels) after DNA repair. Base editors fused to a nickase Cas9 (hereafter referred to as base editors) introduce single base variants, often without frameshifts or indels. They have been used to characterize coding variants17,18,19,20,21 and are valuable when systematically applied to noncoding REs.

In this study, we integrated CRISPRi, dCas9, and base editing with computational predictions to parse noncoding regulatory sequences in the CD69 locus. We identified a ∼170 bp interval within a ∼1,500 bp upstream enhancer that plays a key role in regulating gene expression. Within this interval, base editing and deep learning converge upon a critical C at chr12:9,764,948 (hg38), where a C-to-T transition reduces element accessibility and CD69 expression. We show that this C-to-T base edit ablates a GATA3 binding site, thereby displacing a GATA3-TAL1 activating complex and increasing the association of the BHLHE40 repressor across the element and CD69 promoter. Systematic analysis of chromatin accessibility and TF binding during T cell activation supports a global role for interplay between GATA3 and BHLHE40 in immune gene responses and T cell polarization.

We focused on the CD69 locus, which encodes a key molecule for T cell signal transduction and tissue residency.22,23 CD69 expression is rapidly induced upon stimulation by T cell receptor crosslinking or PMA/ionomycin in both CD4+ T cells and the Jurkat T cell line (Figures S1A and S1B). Chromatin accessibility maps nominated putative regulatory sites that gain accessibility upon stimulation in primary T cells and Jurkat cells (Figure 1B). We complemented these data with predictions from the Enformer model5 trained on chromatin maps and cap analysis of gene expression (CAGE)-seq data.1,24 We also refined the predictions by fine-tuning the Enformer model to predict differential accessibility between resting and stimulated Jurkat cells (Methods). Genomic intervals corresponding to the promoter, an intronic region, the 3′ UTR, and an interval located ∼4 kb upstream of the transcription start site (TSS) were predicted to have a strong impact on CD69 transcriptional induction (Figure 1B).

We used CRISPRi to test the functional impact of seven candidate REs across the CD69 locus, including the promoter (sgProm), the intronic element (sgInt), the predicted upstream element (RE-4), and four other sites in the locus that also gained accessibility upon T cell activation (RE-1, RE-2, RE-3, and RE-5) (Figure 1B; Table S1). We infected Jurkat cells with lentiviral constructs containing KRAB-dCas9 and sgRNAs, selected positive cells with puromycin, applied PMA/ionomycin stimulation, and measured CD69 surface protein expression by flow cytometry. We found that sgRNAs targeting the promoter and RE-4 had the strongest suppressive effects on CD69 induction (Figures 1C and S1C), while sgRNAs targeting the TSS-proximal RE-3 had a weaker effect (Figures 1C and S1C). The impact of the respective CRISPRi perturbations largely correlated with the Enformer predictions (Figure S1D). RE-4 corresponds to a DNase hypersensitive site bound by multiple TFs that has scored in a luciferase reporter assay and a CRISPR activation screen.1,25,26 Whereas chromatin accessibility over RE-4 spans ∼1.4 kb, the Enformer predictions highlighted a specific ∼170 bp sequence interval within RE-4 as most critical for RE-4 accessibility and CD69 expression (Figures 1D and S1E).

To resolve the functional sequences within these elements and test the Enformer prediction, we designed a library of 101 sgRNAs that target sequences across RE-3 and RE-4 (Figures S2A and S2B; Table S2). We began with a pooled dCas9 assay, reasoning that dCas9 would specifically occlude TFs overlapping target sites and thus affect a narrower interval than KRAB-dCas9.27 We infected Jurkat cells with a pooled lentiviral CRISPR library composed of dCas9 and the 101 sgRNAs, selected for puromycin resistance and stimulated with PMA/ionomycin for 5 h. We then isolated genomic DNA from pre-sorted and sorted CD69− and CD69+ subsets (Figure S2C) and amplified the sgRNA cassettes for sequencing. The relative effect of each sgRNA on CD69 expression was calculated based on its enrichment/depletion in CD69+ relative to CD69− libraries. Multiple sgRNAs within the ∼1.7 kb tiled region suppressed CD69 activation (Figures 1E and S2D).

### A single artificial variant alters TF binding patterns and suppresses CD69

We infected Jurkat cells with a CBE vector containing either the top-ranked sgRNA (sg#70), a highly ranked sgRNA in an adjacent interval with several scoring sgRNAs (sg#48), or a control sgRNA (sgCtrl) (Figures 1E, 1F, and 2A). We confirmed that CBE-sg#70 strongly suppressed CD69 induction upon stimulation, while sg#48 had a lower but still significant effect (unpaired t test, p < 0.0001), consistent with our tiling data (Figures 3A and S3A–S3C). In unsorted cells, C-948 was replaced by T on ∼57% of alleles. The proportion of C-948-edited alleles was higher in sorted CD69− Jurkat cells (67%) and lower in the CD69+ population (53.6%), consistent with a suppressive effect on CD69 induction (Figure 3B). ATAC-seq profiles revealed reduced RE-4 accessibility in cells harboring the CBE-sg#70 construct relative to CBE controls (Figures 3C and S3D). The effect was most significant for RE-4 (Figure S3E; false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05; STAR Methods) in the CD69 locus, and we did not observe changes in the vicinity of other activation associated genes such as CD28 and NR4A1 (Figure S3F). We next considered the mechanism that underlies the potent effect of this single base mutation. C-948 directly overlaps a GATA motif predicted by the Enformer model to impact element accessibility in Jurkat cells (Figures 3D and S3G). The C-948-to-T edit disrupts a critical position in this motif. Two adjacent e-box/bHLH motifs were also highlighted by the fine-tuned model gradients, one of which is located at ideal spacing to complete a GATA:TAL1 binding site. Among cognate TFs, GATA3 is highly expressed in Jurkat cells (Figure 3E), up-regulated upon stimulation, and broadly implicated in T cell lineage commitment.30

We therefore used chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) to map GATA3, TAL1, and the enhancer-associated chromatin mark H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac). This confirmed strong binding of GATA3 and TAL1 to RE-4 (Figure 3F). Remarkably, binding of both TFs was entirely lost in sg#70-edited Jurkat cells, consistent with the disruption of the GATA motif. Loss of TF binding was accompanied by reduced accessibility and acetylation in the edited cells. We also confirmed that GATA3 knockout suppressed CD69 induction in stimulated Jurkat cells (Figure S4A), while overexpression of GATA3 or TAL1 increased CD69 induction (Figures S4B and S4C). These data support key roles for the GATA:TAL1 motif and corresponding TFs in CD69 induction, as is consistent with prior studies that have associated these TFs with transcriptional activation in T cells or other hematopoietic lineages.30,31,32,33

### Global interplay between BHLHE40 and GATA3 in T cell responses

Finally, we considered whether BHLHE40 may contribute more broadly to immune gene regulation and T cell phenotypes. We found that BHLHE40 overexpression (OE) led to a global reduction in chromatin accessibility (Figure S5A). BHLHE40 OE also altered the expression of multiple immune genes, up-regulating Th1 and effector T cell-related genes and down-regulating Th2 and naive/stemness pathways (Figures S5B and S5C). ChIP-seq analysis further indicated that BHLHE40 binds REs proximal to many of these deregulated genes, suggesting that the regulation is at least in part direct (Figures S5D and S5E). Notably, the global expression programs associated with BHLHE40 OE are in opposition to those reported for GATA3,31,38,39,40 which is instead implicated in Th2 differentiation (e.g., GATA3, interleukin 21 receptor [IL-21R], IL32) and naive/stemness T cell phenotypes (e.g., BACH2, CD28).

We therefore compared the REs and genes targeted by the respective TFs. First, we evaluated the correspondence in H3K27ac-marked REs bound by the respective TFs genome-wide. This revealed 16,323 GATA3 and 21,146 BHLHE40 sites, with a substantial overlap of 10,623 (28%), consistent with extensive interplay between these TFs (Figure 4E; Table S3). We next collated the set of 5,478 candidate target genes whose promoters were located near bound sites for both factors (STAR Methods; Table S3). These refined targets were also enriched for genes that were responsive to BHLHE40 OE (Figure S5F). However, the co-bound genes were relatively biased toward effector T cell pathways over Th1/Th2 differentiation pathways (Figure 4F). Overall, these data clarify connections from GATA3 and BHLHE40 to several T cell transcriptional programs and in particular support direct roles for the opposing regulators in the rapid transcriptional responses associated with effector T cell biology.

## Discussion

Resolving functional sequences within the vast numbers of putative REs in the human genome is a critical challenge in human genetics. Here, we integrate chromatin maps, deep learning, epigenetic editing, and base editing to parse sequences that control an exemplar inducible gene in Jurkat T cells. Top-scoring base edits clustered in an evolutionarily conserved interval within a CD69 enhancer that was also highlighted by the deep learning model. Integrating regulatory predictions with TF ChIP-seq revealed that these edits disrupt cooperative TAL1 and GATA3 binding, thereby opening the locus to opposing TFs such as BHLHE40. Genome-wide analysis suggests a broader interaction between GATA3 and BHLHE40 in regulating immune genes and T cell phenotypes.

Our results emphasize the importance of epigenetic perturbations and introducing artificial sequence variants for characterizing regulatory sequences, which tend to be highly conserved and may be invisible to methods that rely on natural genetic variation. The approach utilized here also has implications for future studies. First, there remains a considerable gap between the throughput of current approaches and the eventual goal of deciphering the regulatory code of the entire human genome. Functional perturbations will need to be combined with computational approaches, which can help prioritize regions, such as the deep learning model incorporated here. Second, different epigenetic and genetic editing tools may be combined to resolve functional sequences more effectively than either tool alone. Epigenetic perturbations with KRAB-dCas9 allow sensitive identification of putative TF binding regions, which may then be precisely resolved with dCas9 and base editors.

Our study also highlights the interplay between two key TFs, GATA3 and BHLHE40. Two top-scoring C-to-T base edits that suppress the CD69 response both appear to act by shifting the balance away from coordinate GATA3-TAL1 binding toward increased BHLHE40 association with the regulatory sequences. The lack of natural variation makes this region invisible to eQTL and genetic mapping studies, and hence the artificial variants uniquely offer insight into the TFs and motifs underlying its function. Based on their opposing effects at the CD69 locus, we extended our analysis genome-wide and found that the two factors co-regulate a number of immune genes and exert opposing effects on effector T cell function as well as Th1-Th2 differentiation pathways. We speculate that the opposing regulators may be particularly critical to the rapid responsiveness of co-regulated genes during T cell activation.

In conclusion, we have benchmarked emerging experimental and computational strategies to resolve regulatory genomic sequences with increasing precision. Our study demonstrates, in particular, the potential of base editing screens and artificial variants for identifying critical regulatory motifs and TF interactions that underlie rapid and robust transcriptional responses. Further computational and experimental innovations are needed to scale these approaches and further illuminate the syntax of human regulatory genomics.

## Limitations of the study

We also note limitations of our study. Although our pooled screen tested a large number of perturbations, it was limited to a single inducible gene locus in one cell model. Extension of the approach to additional immune loci and primary T cells is an exciting future opportunity. Our approach was also limited by technical aspects of the perturbation tools. The base editor construct is limited by PAM site availability, meaning that we could only edit ∼28% of the Cs or Gs within the targeted REs. Base editors with less restrictive PAM site requirements41 could improve the resolution of future screens. While base editor approaches are mainly focused on C-to-T or A-to-G transitions, prime editors could enable more systematic base changes if they could be applied at scale.42 We also acknowledge that while our study characterizes a set of key regulators acting at the base edit site, it is not exhaustive, and other factors are likely binding the enhancer and impacting CD69 expression.

Finally, we acknowledge several limitations of the Enformer model and its use within this study. First, although the model predictions aided in variant interpretation and hypothesis generation, the biological findings were primarily underpinned by the experimental perturbations. Second, while the model predictions and experimental data highlighted similar intervals and nucleotides, further innovations and more comprehensive evaluations are needed to improve base-level accuracy of the model. In particular, algorithmic improvements, ideally trained in iterative cycles with experimental tests of artificial variants, may ultimately yield sufficiently accurate predictive models to resolve regulatory sequences across the vast noncoding genome. Given the increasing prevalence and potential of deep learning for regulatory genomics, integrative studies such as ours will be critical moving forward.
